435.bp: Democracy depends on citizens encountering diverse viewpoints, but social networks and recommendation algorithms both tend to show people content matching what they already believe. The real problem is not these forces individually but their collision: as social circles reinforce each other and algorithms feed them personalized content, the two create a feedback loop that splinters society into hostile, isolated groups.
435.wh: Most research studies social networks alone or recommender systems alone, treating them as separate mechanisms. In reality they coevolve—your friends influence what content you trust, and algorithms learn which content your friends amplify, then feed it back. Capturing this tangled coupling mathematically without oversimplifying is the bottleneck.
435.ap: Unicoon models users as nodes in a hypergraph (a generalization of networks where a single edge can connect many nodes at once). Social relationships are regular edges, but here's the key: when a recommender algorithm serves trending content to a cohort of similar users, that creates a hyperedge tying all of them together. The framework uses AI agents that simulate both social gossip and algorithmic delivery in real time.
435.wh: A hyperedge captures something a regular graph cannot: the fact that recommender systems instantly synchronize dozens of people around the same trending item, creating a qualitatively different dynamic than pairwise social influence. By letting these two layer together dynamically, the simulation can discover emergent patterns that neither mechanism alone would produce.
435.po: Simulations on real social networks revealed a striking finding: larger social structures paradoxically make small-group polarization worse, not better. The synergy of social and algorithmic feedback accelerates how tightly knit (and ideologically uniform) niche communities become.

436.bp: As AI reasoning models become more transparent by showing their internal reasoning chains, they aim to build user trust. But any information a model exposes can become a security vulnerability. The question is: can an attacker use a model's reasoning traces to figure out whether a particular piece of data was in the training set?
436.wh: Previous membership attacks required access to the model's output scores (its confidence in each prediction). Modern reasoning models don't expose those scores to API users—they expose reasoning text instead. Attackers need a new angle: can they extract membership clues from the reasoning text alone?
436.ap: The researchers noticed that when a model encounters training data it has seen before, its reasoning is confident and organized (like recall), but when it encounters new data, the reasoning is hesitant and exploratory (like figuring something out from scratch). They treat these reasoning chains as points in a semantic space and build an axis running from 'familiar' to 'unfamiliar'. By measuring where a query sample lands on this axis, they predict whether it was in training.
436.ww: A model's reasoning reflects its internal uncertainty. If it has memorized something during training, it reasons about it fluently and directly. If it must reason through something it has never encountered, it shows exploratory, tentative steps. This difference, though subtle in language, creates a measurable pattern in semantic space.
436.po: The framework, called BlackSpectrum, successfully inferred membership on real reasoning models (GPT-4, Llama-2) without needing output scores. This opens a new privacy leak: even 'transparent' reasoning can expose training data membership.

437.bp: In emerging markets, billions of people are getting smartphones but lack literacy and financial security. Predatory apps—fake loan apps, gambling apps, rigged trading platforms—exploit this vulnerability through deliberately unclear permission dialogs and privacy disclosures, stealing money and data from people who cannot protect themselves.
437.wh: Informed consent assumes people read and understand the fine print, but when users have low literacy, language barriers, and time pressure (using phones in noisy environments), this assumption breaks completely. Simultaneously, fixing this through translation alone does not work because the underlying privacy disclosures themselves are often obfuscated deliberately.
437.ap: The researchers collected 50 predatory apps from the Google Play Store and audited their permission disclosures. They then recruited users with low literacy and tested whether they understood app permissions. Finally, they experimented with whether AI-generated summaries, translations into local languages, and visual diagrams could make permissions clearer.
437.ww: Most low-literacy users do not have a mental model of what 'camera permission' or 'contact access' actually means—it is abstract. Concrete, visual explanations paired with translations bypass this gap. An AI can read a permission list and instantly produce a cartoon showing 'this app can see your contacts', which builds intuition where text alone fails.
437.po: The study found that 85% of participants did not understand basic app permissions even after reading. Simple AI-driven summaries and visuals significantly improved comprehension, suggesting that LLM-powered privacy tools could scale protection to millions of vulnerable users.

438.bp: Real-world systems like recommendation engines, social networks, and business databases are not simple graphs with one type of connection. A person and a product might be linked by a purchase, a review, a recommendation, and a share—all different relationships carrying different meanings. Machines need to understand these multifaceted relationships simultaneously.
438.wh: Most methods treat multiple relationship types as independent (sum them up, weight them equally, or process them separately). But relationships actually influence each other: if two users frequently co-purchase items, that trust signal should boost the weight of their mutual recommendations. Simple linear combination misses these mutual promotion and inhibition effects.
438.ap: The researchers propose a learnable matrix that captures how two users connected by one relationship type affect their connection via a different relationship type. They then run this through a graph neural network to aggregate patterns globally, and finally use a decoder that adapts its output based on which specific relationship type each user pair exhibits.
438.ww: By learning a pattern matrix from data, the system discovers which relationship pairs amplify each other (e.g., purchases + recommendations together) and which inhibit each other (e.g., blocking signals that counter trust signals). A hybrid scoring strategy means the final representation respects the unique semantics of each relationship type rather than forcing them into a one-size-fits-all mold.
438.po: Experiments on benchmark datasets for link prediction (guessing missing connections) show the method outperforms baselines that treat relationships independently, especially in dense networks with many overlapping connection types.

439.bp: Drones with cameras are becoming cheap and everywhere—they monitor traffic, crops, construction, and disasters. But drones have tiny onboard processors and batteries, so they run lightweight AI models that often fail on new visual conditions. The system needs to keep these models sharp as the environment changes radically.
439.wh: When a drone moves fast or conditions shift suddenly (clouds, shadows, focus blur), the video footage looks completely different from the training data. Generic continuous learning either retrains too late (by then accuracy already crashed) or falsely detects drift (triggering expensive retraining when it was not needed). Also, the system does not know which old models in the zoo might be useful to reuse, so it retains stale ones.
439.ap: SkyCL detects drift at two levels: immediate pixel-level changes (tells you drift is happening now) and slower prediction-level changes (tells you the old model is becoming unreliable). When drift is detected, instead of retraining on a single drone, it schedules retraining across multiple edge devices in parallel. It also examines historical model relationships to find a hidden improvement path through the model zoo.
439.ww: Dual-level drift detection prevents both false alarms and late reactions. Distributed retraining speeds up model updates so the drone never flies with a stale model for long. Model kinship discovery is key: old models from similar conditions become better starting points for retraining than random initialization.
439.po: Experiments show 14.39% accuracy gain and 2.41× speedup compared to existing methods. Drones maintain usable models under rapid environmental shifts, a critical requirement for real-world deployment.

440.bp: Governments need fine-grained data on poverty, unemployment, and business activity to allocate resources and design policy, but detailed census data is expensive, stale, and protected by privacy laws. Meanwhile, apps like Yelp capture millions of transactions and reviews that encode economic signals. The question is: can you infer high-resolution economic maps from the digital traces businesses and customers leave?
440.wh: Census data is coarse (one number per postal code) and privacy-protected, so you cannot directly map individual blocks. Digital traces are granular but noisy and biased (Yelp users are wealthier and more urban than the general population). Bridging these requires learning a mapping from coarse labels to fine-grained predictions without overfitting to Yelp's specific biases.
440.ap: The method builds a graph where users and businesses are nodes, user-review connections are edges. It learns dense representations of each business informed by the business category (restaurant, bank, etc.) and the neighborhood geography. Crucially, the learning happens only at coarse resolution (postal code labels), but the learned representations capture enough hidden signal to predict at finer block-level resolution.
440.ww: The system discovers that similar businesses in the same neighborhood tend to appear in similar social contexts. A high-end restaurant cluster in one block predicts wealth in adjacent blocks, even though the training only used postal-level labels. The learned representations naturally discover socioeconomic homophily: similar areas group together.
440.po: Experiments on Yelp data show the system infers fine-grained demographics at census block-group resolution with useful accuracy, opening a scalable path to high-resolution economic mapping for policy without privacy violations.

441.bp: AI systems produce fluent, convincing text that looks human-written. As they improve, distinguishing synthetic from real content becomes harder, threatening public trust in information. Understanding what makes people vulnerable to this confusion is essential for defending democratic discourse.
441.wh: Common explanations claim political bias or education level drives susceptibility, but testing this directly is rare. People may be vulnerable not because of who they are demographically but because of how their brains process source information. When text is polished and fluent, it bypasses the cognitive mechanisms that normally flag 'wait, is this trustworthy?'
441.ap: The researchers built two frameworks, JudgeGPT (to generate confusing text) and RogueGPT (to generate deceptive content), then tested 918 human evaluations across five AI models. They applied causal modeling (a formal technique for teasing apart cause from correlation) to identify which factors actually drive detection accuracy.
441.ww: Causal models reveal that fluency is the key. GPT-4 text scores so close to human that people's normal source-monitoring systems fail—the brain thinks 'this is written well, so it must be real' and skips the skepticism step. Conversely, people exposed to past fake news perform better (adversarial training), not because they are smarter but because they learned to distrust fluent narratives.
441.po: Findings show political orientation has almost no impact (r=-0.10), but familiarity with fake news does (r=0.35). The implication: defenses should focus on teaching people to question fluent sources, not on demographic targeting or fact-checking alone.

442.bp: Fake news spreads faster and farther online when it includes images alongside text—the visual component makes false claims feel more real. Detecting these multimodal fakes requires understanding both text and image content together, but labeled datasets are small, noisy, and imbalanced.
442.wh: Traditional fake news detectors trained on text or images separately cannot capture how fake news creators coordinate visuals and language to deceive. Simply stacking text and image models loses the synergy. Standard data augmentation (copying existing data) makes the problem worse by amplifying the dataset's biases. Generative models can create synthetic training data but without guaranteeing the generated images and text actually hang together semantically.
442.ap: MAF-GAN is a generator-discriminator framework that learns to create fake-news samples (images paired with text) in a way that maintains semantic coherence between modalities. It includes a projection module that encodes both text and image, a generator that creates new multimodal fakes, and a discriminator that distinguishes real from synthetic. Importantly, the generator knows the detection task, so it learns to generate realistic hard cases.
442.ww: By training the generator to fool the discriminator on the detection task itself, the framework is forced to learn what makes multimodal fakes convincing. The generated data then becomes high-quality training material: it is diverse, balanced, and hard enough to actually improve detection. Semantic consistency is enforced automatically because the generator learned the relationship between image and text in real fakes.
442.po: Evaluations on four datasets show MAF-GAN outperforms baselines in both accuracy and F1-score (a measure of balance between catching fakes and avoiding false alarms). The framework works particularly well in data-scarce and cross-domain settings where labeled data is limited.

443.bp: Sensors and IoT devices constantly stream time-series data (temperature, stock prices, heartbeats), but real networks drop packets, devices crash, and logging fails. These gaps corrupt downstream analysis—anomaly detection misses signals, recommendations go stale. Filling in missing values accurately is essential for reliable systems.
443.wh: Diffusion models have recently shown promise at this task, but they inject noise uniformly into all frequencies. In real time series, energy is unevenly distributed: low frequencies (slow trends) dominate, high frequencies (rapid noise) are sparse. Treating all frequencies equally means wasting capacity on high-frequency noise and underinvesting in the trends that matter.
443.ap: FSDI analyzes the frequency spectrum (the power across different time scales) of the input data and creates a custom noise schedule per frequency bin. High-energy frequencies (important trends) get less noise injected; low-energy frequencies get more. This is then recalibrated so total noise energy stays constant, preserving the training dynamics of the diffusion model.
443.ww: By matching noise to the true spectral energy distribution, the model invests diffusion capacity where it matters. High-frequency noise is not absorbed into learning useless details; instead, the model focuses on reconstructing the signal structure. This data-driven frequency shaping respects the natural structure of time series rather than forcing a generic schedule.
443.po: Experiments show FSDI significantly outperforms generic diffusion on imputation accuracy, meaning downstream tasks like anomaly detection and recommendations see cleaner data and better performance.

444.bp: Modern web platforms pull information from many sources (text, images, video, metadata), and users often label content with multiple overlapping categories. But real-world data is messy: some sources are missing, and new categories appear constantly. Systems must adapt to both missing data modalities and growing category lists without becoming computationally prohibitive.
444.wh: Existing multi-view multi-label methods fail in two ways: they either cannot handle new classes (they are frozen after training) or they explode in parameters when handling missing views. If you have five data sources and any subset could be missing, that is thirty-two different scenarios to handle independently, leading to exponential parameter bloat.
444.ap: E2PL uses a prompt-based approach (instead of fine-tuning entire models, it appends learned tokens to the input that guide the base model). It has task-tailored prompts for adapting to new classes and missing-aware prompts for handling any subset of missing views. To avoid exponential explosion, it uses tensor decomposition: representing the exponentially many missing scenarios using a compact atomic tensor basis.
444.ww: Tensor decomposition (factoring complex structures into simpler components) reduces the prompt parameter count from exponential in the number of views to linear. This means adding a new view or class requires only incremental parameters, not wholesale model restructuring. Prompts also preserve the base model's knowledge better than retraining.
444.po: Experiments on real web-scale datasets show E2PL handles missing views and incremental class learning simultaneously with far fewer parameters than alternatives, enabling scalable deployment on large platforms.

445.bp: Recommendation systems are moving beyond keyword matching to generative models that compose recommendations from semantic building blocks (like 'Italian cuisine' + 'romantic'). But these semantic blocks are abstract; the system must learn which abstract concepts best summarize users and items while also being useful for generating recommendations.
445.wh: Current methods train the semantic ID codebook (the vocabulary of concepts) and the generator (the recommendation composer) separately. This creates a mismatch: the codebook optimizes for compression (squeezing all knowledge into few IDs) while the generator optimizes for predicting user preferences. Also, when quantizing semantic information, details get lost that could improve recommendations.
445.ap: DOS uses two parallel flows (one for users, one for items) that share signals and align their codebook spaces with the generation space. It also introduces orthogonal residual quantization: when compressing semantic information, it rotates the semantic space to an optimal orientation first, preserving more meaningful information. The method has been deployed in Meituan's production system.
445.ww: By aligning flows, the system ensures semantic codes mean the same thing during training and generation. Orthogonal rotation is a geometric trick: instead of compressing randomly, rotate so the axes align with directions of high semantic variance, preserving signal. Residual quantization (storing errors as additional codes) recovers lost precision.
445.po: Online A/B tests at Meituan (hundreds of millions of users) confirm DOS improves recommendation quality over previous semantic ID methods. The approach is now live, showing real-world impact at scale.

446.bp: AI systems often rely on retrieval-augmented generation: they search for relevant documents, then use those to guide their answers. This works great for factual questions ('Who won the 2020 election?'), where the answer is usually in the retrieved documents. But for predicting preferences ('What product should I recommend?'), the answer is not retrievable—it must be inferred from the user's pattern.
446.wh: Existing RAG systems treat all retrieved documents equally—they dump them into the prompt and hope the AI figure out relevance. For preference prediction, this fails because the relevant signal is the similarity pattern between the user's history and candidate items, not the items themselves. Standard RAG cannot weight by preference-specific relevance.
446.ap: PRAG computes how similar a user's past behavior is to each candidate (using semantic similarity in learned representation space). Instead of treating all documents equally, it weights them by this similarity score when building the prompt. The LLM then sees personalized signals: 'This product is similar to 5 things you liked and different from 2 you disliked'.
446.ww: By directly encoding user-specific patterns into the prompt weights, PRAG turns preference prediction into something retrieval can handle. The retrieval system is no longer asked to find THE answer (it does not exist) but to provide contextual evidence. The weighting makes implicit preferences explicit.
446.po: Experiments on four real recommendation datasets using multiple LLM backbones show PRAG significantly outperforms standard RAG and non-RAG baselines. The framework integrates easily into existing LLM-based recommendation systems.

447.bp: Training data is expensive and private, so researchers increasingly use AI to generate synthetic data. But when models train on synthetic data generated by other models, a dangerous cycle begins: rare features vanish, the distribution shrinks, and the model becomes less creative. This model collapse is a silent killer of dataset quality.
447.wh: Most rare features (the 'tail' of the distribution) appear infrequently in training data. When an AI generates synthetic data, it naturally emphasizes common patterns and under-samples rare ones. If downstream models retrain on this synthetic data, rare features disappear entirely. Iterating this process compresses diversity catastrophically.
447.ap: DASGen identifies underrepresented regions by examining the embedding space (a learned representation of semantic meaning). It then crafts targeted prompts for a frozen LLM to generate new text focusing on those rare regions, guided by a diversity objective. The entire process runs without retraining—prompt engineering only.
447.ww: By targeting tail regions explicitly, DASGen forces the generative process to produce diverse outputs rather than defaulting to high-confidence common cases. Diversity objectives penalize clustering, so the model spreads its output across the semantic space. Freezing the base LLM prevents catastrophic forgetting.
447.po: On Yelp and ICLR reviews, DASGen achieves 98.54% and 92% coverage of tail regions respectively, compared to much lower rates with standard generation. Downstream models trained on DASGen data maintain better accuracy and diversity.

448.bp: Edge devices (sensors, cameras, small compute nodes) form IoT workflows—a camera detects motion, triggers a classifier, which sends an alert. But networks partition, devices fail, and services advertise vague capability descriptions. When a workflow step needs a specific service type and it goes down, the entire workflow fails even though a compatible alternative might exist nearby.
448.wh: Traditional service registries work via exact matching: if you request an 'ImageClassifier' but only a 'FastImageClassifier' is available, the lookup fails. Semantic matching would help (recognizing that FastImageClassifier is a type of ImageClassifier), but replicating semantic registries across partitioned networks is complex. Also, modeling the uncertainty of what is actually available in a dynamic system is hard.
448.ap: SemaReg models each edge device as an AI agent with beliefs (what services are where), desires (success, latency, security), and intentions (active goals). These agents gossip about service availability using an epidemic protocol (each node occasionally shares rumors with neighbors). Semantic type matching (using ontologies—semantic hierarchies) lets a workflow accept a compatible subtype when the exact type is missing.
448.ww: The AI agent framework captures uncertainty: a device does not know if a distant service is truly down or just unreachable due to network partition. Beliefs encode this uncertainty, and agents reason about it when making binding decisions. Gossip is robust to partitions because it requires no central coordinator. Semantic type hierarchies let workflows be flexible without hard-coding all alternatives.
448.po: Simulation of 80 edge devices shows 90% workflow success at moderate partition levels, improving by 43% over naive broadcast discovery. The semantic approach gracefully handles missing primary services.

449.bp: Vision Transformers (large AI models pretrained on millions of images) are powerful, but adapting them to new tasks requires updating billions of weights—computationally expensive on phones and edge devices. If we could adapt them by changing only a small fraction of weights, we could democratize powerful vision AI.
449.wh: Full fine-tuning of a Transformer model for image classification requires thousands of GPU hours and gigabytes of memory. Parameter-efficient tuning trades some accuracy for speed and memory, but different techniques (adding small modules, reweighting, freezing layers, etc.) have different trade-offs. Understanding which approach fits which scenario is hard.
449.ap: This survey reviews five families of parameter-efficient approaches: additive (adding small trainable modules to a frozen base), reparameterization (representing weight updates compactly), selective (fine-tuning only certain layers), hybrid (combining approaches), and inference-efficient (optimizing at prediction time). Each family trades off differently against accuracy and speed.
449.ww: Additive methods preserve pretraining by not touching base weights but add overhead during inference. Selective methods are memory-efficient but may miss important feature interactions. Hybrid approaches often win empirically by combining the strengths of multiple techniques. Inference-efficient methods shift cost away from fine-tuning entirely.
449.po: The survey synthesizes evaluation protocols and benchmarks, showing when each approach excels. It identifies open challenges: how to automate the choice of technique, how to combine methods more elegantly, and how to guarantee robustness across diverse downstream tasks—paving the way for truly practical efficient adaptation.
